note_on_method: These notes are researched, not visited. Nobody working on this directory has played on a Seattle court, and none of the writing below pretends otherwise: there is no crowding, no surface condition, no sense of the place on a Saturday morning, because no source states any of that and inventing it would be the most damaging thing this site could ship. Venue-name searches are read by the people who already know the venue. What each note does contain is what Seattle Parks records about that specific site, where it sits among the twenty-four venues we have verified, and its own correction history: what the imported commercial record claimed and what the city says instead. That last part is genuinely particular to each venue and is the most useful thing we can honestly say about it. Where a reader wants to know what it is actually like to play there, the page says we do not know and points at the correction link.

slots.description: Green Lake Park East is the largest pickleball site Seattle Parks records, with eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball on the east side of the lake, and it is the only one in the city running an organised open-play programme. That programme is what makes it different from every other entry in this directory. Since 1 October 2025 the city has staffed scheduled sessions here with ambassadors who arrange games and run a paddle stacking system, which is a rotation queue: you put your paddle in the stack and get called into the next game rather than needing to arrive as a group of four. It was set up as a one-year pilot, so its future beyond autumn 2026 is not something we can tell you. The courts sit inside Green Lake Park, which is one of the busiest parks in Seattle, and the parking that serves them serves the whole lake path rather than the courts specifically. It is also the venue where our imported record was most wrong, which is worth stating on the page rather than quietly fixing. The commercial dataset we started from listed Green Lake as four courts, two of them indoor. Seattle Parks records eight courts, all outdoor, and there is no indoor pickleball at Green Lake at all. That is a doubling of the court count and the invention of two indoor courts in a city that has none verified, and it is the clearest single illustration of why nothing here publishes until a named source has confirmed it.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records dedicated parking at this site and gives the address as 7201 E Green Lake Dr N. Be careful with that: the lot belongs to Green Lake Park as a whole, and the park draws walkers, runners and rowers all day, so a dedicated lot existing is not the same as a space being free when you arrive. The city publishes no capacity or time-limit information for it and we have not checked restrictions on the ground, so read the posted signs. An all-year restroom is recorded on site.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts with nets provided, no lights, and tennis lines under your feet. If you are coming alone or as a pair, come inside one of the open-play windows — Monday 8 to 10 a.m., Wednesday 1 to 3 p.m., Saturday 9 to 11 a.m., or Sunday 4 to 6 p.m. — because that is when the rotation runs and when getting into a game does not depend on who you brought. Outside those hours it is first come, first served like everywhere else. With no lighting recorded here, play ends when the light does, which in a Seattle December is early.

faqs.q: Can I turn up alone and get a game?
faqs.a: Yes, during the open-play windows, and this is the only Seattle venue where that is a designed feature rather than luck. Ambassadors run a paddle stacking system in those sessions so single players rotate in. Outside those hours you are on your own like anywhere else.

faqs.q: Are these courts indoor?
faqs.a: No. All eight are outdoor, and there is no covered or climate-controlled pickleball recorded anywhere in Seattle. An earlier commercial record claimed two indoor courts here; the city's own data does not, and we have removed the claim.

faqs.q: Is there a fee?
faqs.a: Not verified. Seattle Parks publishes no fee information for its pickleball courts, so we show cost as unverified here as everywhere else on this site rather than assuming it is free.

slots.description: Gilman Playground in Ballard carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is one of three Seattle sites where the city has formally restricted when you may play. In September 2025 Seattle Parks, working with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections, ran noise studies at this location and found play producing sound levels above the limits set in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. The result was a posted schedule with real enforcement behind it rather than a request for consideration. That history is worth knowing before you turn up, because it shapes both when the courts are open and how the neighbours are likely to feel about a loud evening game.
slots.getting_there: The address Seattle Parks records is 923 NW 54th St, and the city records street parking rather than a dedicated lot — this is a residential Ballard block, and no capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for it. A seasonal restroom is recorded, which means do not count on it out of season. We have not verified parking restrictions on the ground; read the signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, and no lights recorded, which matters more here than elsewhere because the posted hours run to 10 p.m. and nothing illuminates the court after dusk. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. Those hours are enforced: a violation captured on timestamped photo or video results in a lock fitted to the courts for at least thirty days, and repeat violations make the lock permanent, after which the courts open only when staff are on site to unlock them. For context on how unusual that is: of the twenty-four verified Seattle venues, only three carry a city-imposed curfew, and Gilman is the smallest of them by court count. Nineteen of the twenty-four have no lighting recorded at all, so for most of the city the limit on evening play is the sunset rather than the council.

faqs.q: What time do the courts close?
faqs.a: 10 p.m. every day, with opening at 7 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. These hours took effect on 15 September 2025.

faqs.q: Why does this park have hours when most do not?
faqs.a: Noise studies run by Seattle Parks with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play here producing sound levels above the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. Gilman is one of three Seattle sites given posted hours as a result.

faqs.q: What happens if people play after 10 p.m.?
faqs.a: The city fits a lock. A violation documented outside posted hours with timestamped visual evidence results in a temporary lock for at least thirty days; repeat violations lead to a permanent lock, after which the courts open only when staff are on site to unlock them.

faqs.q: Are nets provided?
faqs.a: Yes. Seattle Parks records nets at this location, which is not universal — the city records nets at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball sites and says nothing either way about the other eight, so a portable net is worth carrying if you also play elsewhere in the city.

slots.description: Laurelhurst Playfield holds a single dedicated pickleball court — one of only three dedicated courts among the twenty-four Seattle venues we have verified, with every other site striped over tennis or shared with basketball or badminton. Being dedicated is the good news and being one court is the bad news, and the second is the more useful fact when you are deciding whether to drive here. It is also one of three Seattle locations where the city imposed restricted hours in September 2025 after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play exceeding the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. There is one more thing worth knowing, and it is a correction rather than a feature. Our imported record placed this venue at 4339 NE 43rd St. The city's own parcel record puts it at 4544 NE 41st St, two blocks away, and the city is describing land it owns. We have taken the municipal address and left the imported one visible in our change log rather than overwriting history, because a directory that silently corrects itself is asking to be trusted on exactly the thing it just got wrong.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records the address as 4544 NE 41st St, which corrects the address our imported record carried — it had this venue two blocks away on NE 43rd St. Dedicated parking is recorded on site, along with an all-year restroom. The city publishes no capacity or restriction detail, and we have not checked it in person.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, nets provided, no lights. A single court means one game at a time, so on a good weekend afternoon expect either a wait or a rotation negotiated between whoever is there. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, and those hours carry the same enforcement as the other two restricted sites: timestamped evidence of play outside them leads to a lock for a minimum of thirty days, permanent on repeat.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball court?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is rare here. Seattle Parks records only four dedicated pickleball locations in the city and three of them, including this one, have a single court. Every other verified Seattle venue shares its surface with tennis, basketball or badminton.

faqs.q: Only one court — will I get on?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on who else turns up, and we have no crowding data for any Seattle venue so we will not guess. One court means one game at a time and an informal rotation with whoever is waiting.

faqs.q: What time does it close?
faqs.a: 10 p.m., opening 7 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, in force since 15 September 2025 after noise studies found levels above Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08.

faqs.q: Are nets provided, and is there a restroom?
faqs.a: Nets yes, and an all-year restroom is recorded on site, which matters more than it sounds — eleven of the twenty-five Seattle pickleball locations have only a seasonal restroom and three have none recorded at all. Dedicated parking is also recorded here rather than street parking.

slots.description: Mt. Baker Park carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is the only one of the three restricted-hours sites that also has lights — which is an odd combination worth understanding before you plan an evening around it. The city recorded lighting here, and then in September 2025 capped play at 10 p.m. after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found sound levels above the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. So the lights exist and the clock still stops. Of the five lit venues among our twenty-four verified Seattle sites, this is the one where the lights are least useful late. Our imported record also had this venue's address as a street with no number — just Lake Park Dr S — which is the kind of gap that looks harmless until someone tries to drive to it. The city's parcel record supplied 2521, and that is the number shown above.
slots.getting_there: The address Seattle Parks records is 2521 Lake Park Dr S; our imported record had the street with no number, and the city's own parcel record supplied it. Street parking rather than a dedicated lot, on a residential block above Lake Washington, with an all-year restroom recorded on site. No permit or time-limit information is published and we have not verified restrictions in person.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts with nets provided and lights, open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. The enforcement here is the same as at Gilman and Laurelhurst: play documented outside posted hours with timestamped visual evidence results in a lock for at least thirty days, and further violations make it permanent. If you want lit courts without a curfew, Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield are the two larger lit sites with no restricted-hours order recorded against them. One practical note on the curfew that applies to all three restricted sites: the enforcement trigger is documented evidence rather than a complaint, so it is timestamped photos and video that lead to a lock, not annoyance on its own. That distinction is in the city's own announcement and it is the reason the posted hours are worth taking literally here in a way they are not at an unlit park that empties at dusk anyway.

faqs.q: It has lights — can I play late?
faqs.a: Until 10 p.m. and no later. This is the only Seattle venue that is both lit and curfewed, so the lights are genuinely useful in winter afternoons and genuinely capped at night. For lit courts without a posted curfew, Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield carry no such order in the records we have checked.

faqs.q: Why is there a curfew at a lit park?
faqs.a: The two are unrelated. The lighting is recorded by Seattle Parks as a facility; the hours were imposed in September 2025 after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play exceeding Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08.

faqs.q: Where do I park?
faqs.a: Street parking — Seattle Parks records no dedicated lot here. No permit or time-limit information is published and we have not checked restrictions on the ground, so read the posted signs.

slots.description: Bitter Lake Playfield holds eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball under lights, which makes it one of exactly two sites in Seattle offering both the largest court count and evening play. Between it and Rainier Beach Playfield sit sixteen of the ninety-two verified courts in the city, and they carry most of the practical capacity for playing here once the light goes. It is also the venue our imported data handled worst. The commercial dataset we started from held two separate Bitter Lake entries: a community centre with three indoor courts, and a second row claiming eleven courts of which three were indoor. Seattle Parks records one pickleball site at this address, with eight courts, all outdoor. We matched the outdoor row and left the community centre alone, because the centre is a building with its own indoor courts and merging the two would have invented a fifteen-court complex that does not exist anywhere except in a spreadsheet.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records the address as 13035 Linden Ave N and gives this site dedicated parking rather than street parking, which among the twenty-four verified venues puts it in the better-served half. The restroom is recorded as seasonal, so it is not something to count on outside the warm months. No capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for the parking, and none of it has been checked on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts, nets provided, and lights: the fullest combination available in Seattle on the city's own record. The courts are shared with tennis, so expect tennis lines underfoot and the possibility of a booked court, which is true of eighteen of the twenty-five sites Seattle Parks lists. There is no posted-hours order against this location in the records we have checked, unlike Gilman, Laurelhurst and Mt. Baker, so the lights are not capped by a curfew. Seattle Parks publishes no crowding or peak-time data for any venue, so we cannot tell you when it fills.

faqs.q: Is this the same place as Bitter Lake Community Center?
faqs.a: No, and keeping them apart mattered. The community centre is a building with three indoor courts of its own; this record is the outdoor playfield with eight. They share a campus. Our imported data blurred the two into a single eleven-court entry, which the city records do not support.

faqs.q: Can I play here in the evening?
faqs.a: The city records lighting here, and no restricted-hours order applies to this site in the records we have checked. What Seattle Parks does not publish is when the lights actually run or whether they are switched on seasonally, so treat evening play as possible rather than guaranteed.

faqs.q: Are the courts dedicated to pickleball?
faqs.a: No. This is a shared tennis and pickleball surface, which is the norm in Seattle. Only four of the twenty-five locations the city records are dedicated pickleball, and three of those are single courts.

faqs.q: How does it compare with Rainier Beach?
faqs.a: They are the two eight-court lit sites in Seattle and between them hold sixteen of the city's ninety-two verified courts. Rainier Beach has an all-year restroom where Bitter Lake's is seasonal; both have dedicated parking and nets. On the city's record the two are close to interchangeable, and the deciding factor for most people will be which end of Seattle they are starting from.

slots.description: Rainier Beach Playfield carries eight lit courts striped for tennis and pickleball, tying it with Bitter Lake for the largest lit site in the verified Seattle set. It is also the one venue where our imported record and the city agreed exactly, which is rare enough here to be worth stating: the commercial dataset said eight outdoor courts and Seattle Parks says eight outdoor courts. Across the twenty matched Seattle venues, sixty-two imported values were overwritten by the municipal record, so exact agreement on a court count is the exception rather than the rule. The match still needed a decision, because the same import also held a Rainier Beach Community Center row claiming three indoor courts. That is a different venue, a building with its own courts, and it is not published here.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives the address as 4707 S Cloverdale St and records dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, the better of the two restroom categories the city uses. Eleven of the twenty-five sites in the dataset have an all-year restroom, eleven are seasonal, and three have none recorded at all. No permit or time-limit detail is published, and none of it has been verified on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts with nets provided and lights, shared with tennis. No restricted-hours order is recorded against this site, so unlike Mt. Baker the lights are not paired with a 10 p.m. curfew. Combined with dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, this is one of the better-equipped venues in the city on the record, though equipped is not the same as quiet and nothing is published about how busy any court gets. The gaps are the standard Seattle ones: no surface type, no fee and no published hours for the site, so those rows read as unverified rather than being filled from a commercial record that had no source behind them either.

faqs.q: Is this the community centre?
faqs.a: No. Seattle Parks records the playfield and the community centre separately, and this page is the playfield: eight outdoor courts. The community centre entry in our import claims three indoor courts and has not been verified, so it does not appear on this site at all.

faqs.q: Did anything change from the original data?
faqs.a: Almost nothing, which is unusual here. The court count and the outdoor split both matched the city record exactly. The address was corrected, and everything the city does not state, including surface, fees and hours, was cleared to unverified.

faqs.q: Are there lights and a restroom?
faqs.a: Both are recorded by the city: lighting present, and an all-year restroom rather than a seasonal one. What is not recorded anywhere is the hours those lights operate.

faqs.q: How does it compare with Bitter Lake?
faqs.a: They are the only two eight-court lit venues in the city and are near-identical on the record: nets, dedicated parking, lights, tennis-shared. The one difference Seattle Parks records is the restroom, all-year here and seasonal at Bitter Lake, which is a small thing in July and a real one in January. Neither carries a posted-hours order.

slots.description: West Magnolia Playfield is one of four venues on this site that our imported dataset did not contain at all. Eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball, dedicated parking, an all-year restroom: a substantial site by any reading, and the commercial directory we started from had no row for it. It exists here only because we went to the city's own pickleball dataset rather than trusting the import, and that is the argument for municipal sourcing in a single example. It is the largest unlit site in Seattle, sharing the eight-court tier with Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Green Lake East but without their evening option. We deliberately did not match it to Magnolia Community Center, which is a nearby indoor building with three courts of its own and a genuinely different venue.
slots.getting_there: The Parks record gives 2518 34th Ave W, with dedicated parking and an all-year restroom. Because this venue was minted from municipal data rather than matched to an imported row, every fact on this page including the address comes from the city, and nothing at all came from the commercial import. No capacity or restriction information is published and none has been checked in person.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts, nets provided, no lights recorded. That combination makes it the largest daylight-only site in the city: plenty of capacity, and nothing to extend it past dusk, which in a Seattle December means play ends before half past four. Shared with tennis, like most Seattle courts. No crowding data is published for this or any other venue, so we cannot tell you whether eight courts is enough on a Saturday. As a minted venue its gaps are the city's gaps: no surface type, no fee, no hours and no indication of demand on what is jointly the largest court count in Seattle. Eight courts with no lighting is a specific and slightly awkward combination, offering the most capacity in the city during hours when capacity is least likely to be the binding constraint. We have not been to see whether that plays out.

faqs.q: Why was this venue missing from other directories?
faqs.a: We can only speak for the commercial dataset we imported, which had no row for it. Seattle Parks does record it. That gap is the reason this project treats a municipal source as the starting point rather than as a cross-check on someone else's list.

faqs.q: Is this Magnolia Community Center?
faqs.a: No. The community centre is an indoor building nearby with three courts, recorded separately. We deliberately did not merge them, because merging a playfield with a building is how a directory ends up publishing a court count that belongs to neither.

faqs.q: Are there lights?
faqs.a: No. Seattle Parks records no lighting here, and unlike a venue where the city is simply silent, this is a positive record of absence.

faqs.q: Is eight courts a lot for Seattle?
faqs.a: It is the joint maximum. Four sites in the city have eight courts and nothing has more: this one, Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Green Lake East. Of those four, two are lit and two are not, and West Magnolia is in the unlit half. So this is as much daytime capacity as Seattle offers in one place.

slots.description: Miller Playfield on Capitol Hill carries five courts under lights, which makes it the largest lit site in the centre of the city. The other four lit venues sit in Ballard, Rainier Beach, West Seattle and at Mt. Baker. Seattle Parks names the parcel Pendleton Miller Playfield. Our imported record claimed four courts; the city says five, and on a five-court site a missing court is a twenty per cent error on the single number people most want. The match also needed care, because the same import held a separate Miller Community Center row at the same 330 19th Ave E address, claiming seven courts of which three were indoor. That is the building beside the playfield, not these courts, and we did not merge them. Doing so would have produced a twelve-court Capitol Hill complex out of two records describing different things.
slots.getting_there: The address is 330 19th Ave E, which the import and the city agreed on. Dedicated parking and an all-year restroom are both recorded. The playfield sits inside a dense residential grid, and while the city records a dedicated lot it publishes nothing about its size or its restrictions, and we have not looked.
slots.what_to_expect: Five courts, nets provided, lights, shared with tennis. No restricted-hours order applies here in the records we have checked, so the lights are not capped by a curfew the way Mt. Baker's are. For anyone in the centre of Seattle this is the only lit option that is not a substantial drive, which is a statement about the city's provision rather than about this venue. As everywhere, no peak-time or crowding information is published. The remaining gaps are the ones Seattle carries everywhere: no surface type, no fee and no published hours for this site, so those rows read as unverified above.

faqs.q: Is this the same as Miller Community Center?
faqs.a: No, and they share an address, which is exactly why the distinction matters. The community centre is the indoor building; this is the outdoor playfield with five courts. Our import held both, and treating them as one venue would have doubled the apparent capacity of the block.

faqs.q: How many courts are there, really?
faqs.a: Five. The imported record said four. Seattle Parks, which operates the site, records five, and a city record wins on a fact about its own facility.

faqs.q: Why is it called Pendleton Miller Playfield on some maps?
faqs.a: That is the name on the city's parcel record. The pickleball dataset calls the same site Miller Playfield, and we use the shorter form the pickleball layer uses.

faqs.q: Why does the court count matter so much here?
faqs.a: Because the site is small enough that one court is a large fraction of it. Our imported record said four and the city says five; on an eight-court playfield that would be a rounding error, but on a five-court site it is twenty per cent of the capacity. Venue-name searches are read by people who already know the venue, and they are exactly the readers who would notice.

slots.description: Delridge Playfield holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in West Seattle, and it is a good example of how far an unverified record can drift. Our imported dataset claimed seven courts here, three of them indoor. Seattle Parks records four courts, all outdoor, and there is no verified indoor pickleball at this site or anywhere else in the city. So the import overstated the capacity by three courts and invented an indoor facility. The address was wrong as well, by roughly a block on the same street. Neither error is dramatic on its own; together they are the reason this page is built from the city record rather than from the import. We also kept this separate from the Delridge Community Center row, which is the indoor building nearby.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 4458 Delridge Way SW; our imported record had 4501, about a block north. The city record is the property owner describing its own parcel, so it wins. Dedicated parking is recorded, along with a seasonal restroom, which means present in the warm months and not something to plan around in February. No restrictions have been checked on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights. Shared with tennis, so expect tennis lines and the possibility of a booked court. With no lighting recorded, play here is bounded by daylight, and Seattle daylight in midwinter ends before half past four. There is no crowding data published for this venue any more than for the others. What we cannot tell you about Delridge is anything the city does not record, and on this venue that list is long: no surface type, no resurfacing history, no fee, no opening hours, and nothing about whether four courts is enough on a Saturday. The corrected court count and the corrected address came from Seattle Parks; everything the commercial record asserted beyond those was cleared rather than carried over, because a value with no source behind it is worse than an admitted gap. If you play here regularly, the surface condition and the busy hours are exactly the two things a reader would most want and exactly the two we have no honest way to supply.

faqs.q: Are there indoor courts at Delridge?
faqs.a: Not at this venue. Our imported record claimed three and the city records none. There is a Delridge Community Center nearby which is an indoor building, but it has not been verified against a named source, so it does not appear on this site.

faqs.q: How many courts are there?
faqs.a: Four, all outdoor, per Seattle Parks. The imported record said seven. That is the largest single court-count correction in the Seattle set after Green Lake.

faqs.q: Which address is right?
faqs.a: 4458 Delridge Way SW, from the city's parcel record. Our import had 4501 Delridge Way SW, about a block away.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere lit nearby in West Seattle?
faqs.a: Alki Playground is the lit option in West Seattle, with four courts and street parking. Walt Hundley Playfield is also close and also unlit. Of the twenty-four verified Seattle venues only five have lighting recorded at all, so the choice in any one part of the city is usually narrow.

slots.description: Alki Playground carries four lit courts striped for tennis and pickleball, one of only five lit venues among the twenty-four verified in Seattle. It sits in West Seattle above the Alki shoreline. The correction here is not about numbers, which is unusual in this set: the court count and the address both matched the city record exactly. It is about classification. Our imported record typed this venue as a dedicated pickleball facility. Seattle Parks records it as a park whose courts are shared between tennis and pickleball, which is a materially different thing to arrive at with a paddle and an expectation. The city's typing is the one published here, and the imported claim is the kind of small upgrade that unsourced directory data applies to itself without anyone deciding to.
slots.getting_there: The address is 5817 SW Lander St, which the import and the city agreed on exactly. Seattle Parks records street parking rather than a dedicated lot, and a seasonal restroom. Street parking near a shoreline destination is worth knowing about in principle; in practice the city publishes no capacity or restriction data for it and we have not checked, so read the posted signs rather than trusting an assumption.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, lights, shared with tennis. No posted-hours order is recorded against this site. Among the five lit Seattle venues this is the only one with street rather than dedicated parking, which is the practical trade-off to weigh against Bitter Lake or Rainier Beach if you are driving to an evening game. No crowding information is published for any of them, here included. Beyond the recorded facts we know very little about Alki. The city publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours and no indication of how the courts fill on a summer weekend at a beachfront park, which is the one question a reader arriving here would most want answered. We have not been. The imported record did carry claims on some of those fields, and we cleared them rather than republishing them under a municipal badge they had not earned, which is why several rows above read as unverified on a venue that is otherwise well documented.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball facility?
faqs.a: No, despite what some listings say. Our imported record classified it that way; Seattle Parks records a shared tennis and pickleball surface. Expect tennis lines and shared use.

faqs.q: Is there parking at the courts?
faqs.a: The city records street parking rather than a dedicated lot here. It publishes nothing about capacity, permits or time limits, and we have not verified any of that in person.

faqs.q: Are there lights?
faqs.a: Yes, recorded by Seattle Parks, making this one of five lit venues in the verified Seattle set. The city does not publish what hours those lights run.

faqs.q: Is it the best lit option in West Seattle?
faqs.a: It is the only one. Seattle Parks records five lit venues across the city and Alki is the West Seattle entry; Delridge and Walt Hundley, the other two West Seattle sites we have verified, both have no lighting recorded. The trade-off is parking, which is street here rather than the dedicated lots at Bitter Lake and Rainier Beach.

slots.description: Beacon Hill Park holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball. Its distinguishing feature in our records is a naming disagreement inside the city's own data: Seattle Parks calls the parcel BEACON HILL PLAYGROUND in its property record while the pickleball layer calls the same site Beacon Hill Park. Both are the city, both describe the same courts at the same address, and they do not agree with each other. We publish the pickleball layer's name because that is the record describing these courts specifically, and we note the disagreement rather than picking silently. Our imported record offered a third variation, Beacon Hill Playground Tennis Courts, which drops pickleball from the name of a pickleball venue entirely.
slots.getting_there: The address is 1902 13th Ave S, which the import and both city records agree on. Seattle Parks records street parking and a seasonal restroom. The courts sit inside a dense residential neighbourhood; the city publishes no parking capacity or restriction detail and nobody here has checked the signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. With no lighting this is a daylight venue, which for a large part of the Seattle year makes it a lunchtime and weekend court rather than an after-work one. Nothing is published about how busy it gets, and we will not guess. The gaps on this venue are the usual ones and worth naming rather than leaving as blank rows. Seattle Parks records no surface type for any of its pickleball courts, so we cannot tell you whether the asphalt here is recent or cracked. It records no fee, so the cost line reads as unverified even though a municipal park court is very likely free. It records no hours for this site, and nothing at all about how busy four shared courts get on a weekday evening in a dense neighbourhood. Those are real questions and we have no sourced answer to any of them.

faqs.q: Is it Beacon Hill Park or Beacon Hill Playground?

faqs.q: Is there parking?
faqs.a: The city records dedicated parking, though it serves the whole playfield rather than the court specifically. No capacity or restriction data is published.

faqs.q: Is there a better option nearby?
faqs.a: Miller Playfield is the closest substantial venue, with five courts under lights on Capitol Hill, and it is a tennis-shared surface rather than a basketball-shared one. For anyone deciding between them on the record alone, Miller offers more courts, lights and a confirmed net; Montlake offers one court whose net provision the city does not state.

slots.description: South Park Playground holds a single dedicated pickleball court, one of only four dedicated sites in the city and one of three that consist of exactly one court. It is also the venue with the largest address disagreement in the Seattle set. The imported record placed it at 8319 8th Ave S. Seattle Parks places its own parcel at 738 S Sullivan St. Those are not neighbouring numbers on one street; they are different streets, and only one of them is where the city says its land is. We publish the municipal address, because the city is describing property it owns, and the imported address stays visible in the change log rather than being quietly replaced.
slots.getting_there: The address is 738 S Sullivan St, corrected from the imported 8319 8th Ave S as described above. Seattle Parks records dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, which for a one-court site is better provision than most. No capacity or restriction detail is published and none has been checked on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, nets provided, no lights, dedicated to pickleball rather than shared. For a single court that is a good specification: real markings, a net on site, parking and a year-round restroom. The constraint is simply that there is one of it, so a busy afternoon is a queue. The city publishes nothing about how busy it gets. What we cannot tell you is what the surface is, what it costs, when it is open, and whether one court is enough on any given afternoon. Those rows read as unverified above. The address correction is the substantive thing this page contributes: an imported record placing a venue on the wrong street is not a small error for a single-court site somebody has to find. One court puts this among the eight smallest venues in the city, though it is one of only four with dedicated pickleball markings rather than borrowed ones.

faqs.q: Which address is correct?
faqs.a: 738 S Sullivan St, from the city's parcel record. Our imported record had 8319 8th Ave S, which is a different street. Where a city describes land it owns and a commercial dataset disagrees, the city wins.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball court?
faqs.a: Yes. Seattle Parks records the use type as pickleball rather than shared. Only four of the twenty-five locations in the city dataset are recorded that way.

faqs.q: Are nets provided?
faqs.a: Yes, the city records nets at this location.

faqs.q: Why does the address correction matter so much here?
faqs.a: Because a single-court venue is hard enough to find without being sent to the wrong street. Our imported record placed this site at 8319 8th Ave S; Seattle Parks places its own parcel at 738 S Sullivan St. On an eight-court playfield an address error is an inconvenience. On one dedicated court it is the difference between a session and a wasted trip, and it is the kind of error that never surfaces in a spreadsheet because both values look equally plausible until someone checks one of them against the operator's own record.

slots.description: Greenwood Park holds a single court shared with basketball, and it arrived here through the back door. Our imported dataset had no row for it at all, so like Maple Leaf, West Magnolia and Walt Hundley it exists on this site only because we read the city's pickleball dataset directly. It then produced the one naming problem we had to solve against the city rather than against the import: the pickleball layer spells the park Greenwod, dropping a letter, while the Parks property record for the same parcel spells it GREENWOOD PARK. Two municipal records, one park, two spellings. We publish the Parks spelling and record the correction, on the same principle that governs the misspelled street at Kinnear Park.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 602 N 87th St and records street parking with a seasonal restroom. Because this venue was minted from municipal data rather than matched to an imported row, the address and every other fact above came from the city. No parking capacity or restriction information is published and none has been checked.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, no lights, shared with basketball, and nets not recorded either way. That is the same specification as Montlake Playfield, and the same advice applies: on a basketball-shared surface with no net recorded, a portable net is worth having. One court means one game at a time. The city publishes no availability data for this or any other Seattle venue. Beyond the corrected name, this is a thin record and the page does not pretend otherwise. Seattle Parks does not state whether nets are provided on a basketball-shared court, which is the gap that matters most here for the same reason it matters at Montlake. It publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours and nothing about demand. One shared court with no net recorded is a venue to check on before travelling, and we have no way to check it for you from a desk. One shared court puts this at the smallest end of the Seattle set, alongside Kinnear Park, Montlake Playfield, Laurelhurst Playfield and South Park Playground, which are the other single-court sites we have verified.

faqs.q: Is it Greenwood or Greenwod?
faqs.a: Greenwood. The city's pickleball dataset spells it Greenwod, dropping a letter; the Parks property record for the same parcel spells it correctly. We publish the correct spelling and record that we corrected it.

faqs.q: Why is this venue not on other directories?
faqs.a: We can only speak for the commercial dataset we imported, which had no row for it. It is here because the city records it.

faqs.q: Are nets provided?
faqs.a: Unknown. Seattle Parks does not record nets at this location, and we do not read an absent record as a no.

faqs.q: What else is nearby?
faqs.a: Bitter Lake Playfield is the substantial northern option, with eight courts under lights, nets, dedicated parking and a seasonal restroom. Against that, Greenwood is a single basketball-shared court with no net recorded, and the honest comparison is that the two are not really in the same category.
